<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Jahana Hayes, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: Pursuant to current law, both applications for grants from the Secretary to a state applicant and applications for subgrants from states to eligible applicants must utilize a peer review process.\29\ H.R. 7082 would still require the Secretary to use the peer review process in evaluating grant applications by states, but states would no longer be required to utilize the peer review process in evaluating subgrant applications by eligible applicants.\30\ This would provide tremendous leeway to states when choosing subgrant recipients without the benefit of the critical, impartial, and knowledgeable quality control and standards of peer review.
\29\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221b(d)(2).
\30\H.R. 7082 Sec. 3, 119th Cong. (2026).
H.R. 7082 Would Weaken Requirements of Subgrant
Applications to State Entities
Current law requires state entities, in their application for a grant, to describe how the state entity will determine and award competitive subgrants, including how it will evaluate applications for subgrants and certain requirements that subgrant applications must include.\31\ H.R. 7082 would depart from this by permitting state entities to accept an application for becoming a charter school within the state ``in lieu of'' an application for a subgrant, as long as state laws for becoming a charter school are met.\32\ In other words, if state law requirements for becoming a charter are more lenient than the federal law requirements for a subgrant, then the federal requirements may be ignored. For example, federal law currently requires that applicants for subgrants describe how they will include parent and community input about the charter school; however, if a state does not require this, and it chooses to use an eligible applicant's application to be a charter school, then that requirement would no longer be necessary. This change would eliminate important aspects of subgrant applications, allow state laws to trump federal requirements that Congress deemed necessary to receive a subgrant, and create inconsistency in the application process across states.
\31\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221b(f)(1).
\32\H.R. 7082 Sec. 3, 119th Cong. (2026).
H.R. 7082 Would Eliminate Consistency in Planning
Current law permits subgrantees to use up to 18 months for planning purposes.\33\ H.R. 7082 would eliminate this and leave the amount of planning time up to each state, though it may not exceed two years.\34\ This would eliminate consistency in the program across states lines. Moreover, some management organizations operate in more than one state; therefore, it's possible that this change could potentially lead to inconsistency in their ability to plan accordingly.
\33\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221b(d)(1)(B).
\34\H.R. 7082 Sec. 3, 119th Cong. (2026).
H.R. 7082 Would Open the Door for Significant Additional
and Extended Expenditures
Current CSP law contains numerous provisions to help plan for, open a new, or replicate or expand a high-quality charter school, but federal funding for these supports is short term. This requires charter schools and management organizations to plan for alternative financial support in the long-term. H.R. 7082 would flip this model on its head. Current law permits subgrant funding to be used for hiring and compensation for teachers, school leaders, and specialized instructional support personnel during the planning period of the grant.\35\ H.R. 7082 would eradicate the limited time period and instead permits funding to be used for compensation throughout the grant period.\36\ Similarly, current law permits funding to be used for ``one-time, startup costs associated with providing transportation to students to and from the charter school.''\37\ H.R. 7082 would eliminate the restriction for ``one-time, startup,'' enabling funding to be used for transportation throughout the grant period.\38\ Current law also permits the use of funding for certain ``appropriate, non-sustained costs'' when funding is not otherwise available.\39\ H.R. 7082 would similarly jettison the limitation on the use of funds for those other costs.\40\
\35\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221b(h)(1)(B).
\36\H.R. 7082 Sec. 3, 119th Cong. (2026).
\37\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221b(h)(4).
\38\H.R. 7082 Sec. 3, 119th Cong. (2026).
\39\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221b(h)(6).
\40\H.R. 7082 Sec. 3, 119th Cong. (2026).
H.R. 7082 would also add a provision to allow subgrant funding to be used for ``necessary renovations, upgrades, or facilities repairs, or acquiring portable classrooms.''\41\ This would constitute an expansion of facilities language into the high-quality charter schools section of the program rather than the section devoted to facilities financing assistance. Moreover, it is unclear how necessity would be determined. Facilities related spending can be costly, and there is no limit included in the new provision, so the funding could eat up the entire allocation for the high-quality charter schools section of the program. Furthermore, the use of portable classrooms raises questions about health and safety for students and teachers.\42\ H.R. 7082 would also add a provision that would permit funding for ``costs associated with operations and management of the charter school facility.''\43\ As written, it is unclear if this means the physical facility itself, or the entire existence of the charter school. Either way, there are no limits on this new provision.
\41\Id.
\42\Here & Now, Portable Classrooms No Place to Learn, Critics Say, Nat'l Pub. Radio (May 9, 2014, 12:50 PM), https://www.npr.org/ transcripts/311103104#: :text=Portable%20classrooms %20are%20a%20quick%20fix%20for,more%20to%20maintain%20as%20they%20get%20 older.
\43\H.R. 7082 Sec. 3, 119th Cong. (2026).
Overall, these changes would establish a reliance on subgrant funding for the duration of the subgrant and would not require or even encourage charter schools or management organizations to plan for continuity and self-sustainment once the subgrant period ends, potentially exacerbating the existing problem of charter schools that either never open or open only to close shortly thereafter.
Changes to the National Activities Section of CSP May Lead to Greater
Waste, Fraud, and Abuse
H.R. 7082 Would Allow for Significantly Increased Funding for Charter
Management Organizations and the Potential for Waste, Fraud,
and Abuse
Currently, the bulk of funding under the national activities section of CSP flows to eligible entities, which are defined as charter management organizations--organizations that manage charter schools. H.R. 7082 would permit the Secretary to more than double the amount of funding that may be used for national activities, significantly increasing the amount of money these organizations may receive. This increase in funding to charter management organizations is problematic because of allegations and reports of waste, fraud, and abuse in CSP.
A2016 audit by the Department's Office of Inspector General (OIG) concluded that charter school relationships with charter management organizations lacked strong internal controls and oversight related to conflicts of interest, insufficient segregation of duties, and related-party transactions. This increased the risks of: lack of accountability of federal funds; waste, fraud, and abuse; and schools not providing students the services required by federal programs.\44\ Additionally, a 2022 OIG audit found that for CSP funds distributed between 2013 and 2016, grantees (including management organizations) opened or expanded only 51 percent of the schools promised and for which they received funding.\45\ Most recently, a 2023 OIG audit found that charter management organizations did not always address compliance issues relating ``to their uses of Replication and Expansion grant funds, fiscal control, and fund accounting'' and that charter schools ``with highly problematic applications'' still received millions of federal dollars from CSP.\46\ It is also worth noting that the National Center for Charter School Accountability recently reported identifying ``$858 million wasted due to fraud, theft, profiteering, or incompetence.\47\
\44\U.S. Dep't of Educ., Off. of Inspector Gen., Nationwide Assessment of Charter and Education Management Organizations--Final Audit Report at 2 (Sept. 2016), https://www.oversight.gov/sites/ default/files/oig-reports/a02m0012.pdf.
\45\U.S. Dep't of Educ., Off. of Inspector Gen., Effectiveness of Charter School Programs in Increasing the Number of Charter Schools at 3 (Sept. 21, 2022), https://www.oversight.gov/sites/default/files/oig-reports/ED/FY22A21IL0034020724v100SECURED.pdf.
\46\U.S. Dep't of Educ., Off. of Inspector Gen., The U.S. Department of Education's Processes for Overseeing Charter Schools Program Grants to Charter Management Organizations for the Replication and Expansion of High-Quality Charter Schools at 2 (Aug. 3, 2023), https://oig.ed.gov/sites/default/files/reports/202403/ FY23A18IL0009012924SECUREDv100.pdf.
\47\Nat'l Ctr. for Charter Sch. Accountability and Network for Pub. Educ., Charter School Reckoning: Decline, Disillusionment and Cost, Part II: Disillusionment at 7 (Dec. 2025), https://networkforpubliceducation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/ Charter-School-Reckoning- Disillusionment.pdf.
H.R. 7082 would do nothing to address these problems, yet it would more than double the amount of funding that could go to charter management organizations, thereby increasing the potential scale of any waste, fraud, and abuse.
H.R. 7082 Would Reduce Understanding of the Overall Impact
of Charter Schools
Under current law, at least 11 percent of funding under national activities must be used for technical assistance, disseminating best practices, and evaluating the impact of CSP, including on student achievement.\48\ H.R. 7082 would reduce this amount to not more than ten percent.\49\ At the same time, the legislation would expand the allowable uses of those limited funds to include funding and financing for charter school facilities, early-stage charter school planning, and grants made by the Secretary to state entities.\50\ In so doing, the legislation would effectively eliminate any requirement that the funding be used to disseminate best practices or evaluate the impact of CSP, thus eliminating transparency about the health and effectiveness of the overall program.
\48\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221d(a).
\49\H.R. 7082 Sec. 4, 119th Cong. (2026).
\50\Id.
H.R. 7082 Would Eliminate the Requirement to Plan for
Financial Sustainability
Under current law, an eligible entity applying for a grant under national activities must include in its application a description of how it will continue to sustain itself after the grant period is over, including a ``multi-year financial and operating model.''\51\ H.R. 7082 would eliminate the requirement for a multi-year model.\52\ This is yet another example of how the bill would provide charter school funding without incentivizing or even encouraging long term success and would further widen the door for school finance challenges and school closures.
\51\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221d(b)(3)(B)(iii).
\52\H.R. 7082 Sec. 4, 119th Cong. (2026).
H.R. 7082 Would Prioritize Grants that Focus on Charter
Management Organizations Rather than Students
